findings.text: Virtual memory event accounting exists in two build shapes. When active it maintains processor-local tallies that callers bump by one or by an arbitrary amount, with separate entry points for contexts that already suppress migration versus contexts that need protection. When inactive all increment, bulk update, aggregation and per-processor folding operations are inert and report nothing.

Specialized wrappers for locality, address-space shootdown and lock statistics either forward to the generic event accounting or expand to empty statements that optionally discard their value argument, depending on build selection. A zone-indexed helper derives a zone-specific event selector by shifting a base selector by the distance between the requested zone identifier and the normal zone.

Zone and node accounting updates two levels at once: a descriptor-local counter and a process-wide aggregate for the same statistic, covering both occupancy and locality event families. Readers of the aggregates and of single-zone occupancy clamp transient negative observations to zero on multiprocessor builds, while one monotonic node reader exposes the raw signed value directly as unsigned.

One zone occupancy reader combines the stored base value with outstanding per-processor differences gathered across online processors before applying the same non-negative clamp. Separately, locality events can be recorded directly into the per-processor portion anchored by a zone descriptor, supporting both unit and delta forms without touching the global aggregate immediately.

Modification helpers provide a layered adjustment interface for zone and node occupancy. Zone adjustments forward a signed delta, while node adjustments first normalize byte-oriented quantities into whole pages after checking alignment. Single-step increment and decrement conveniences exist for both levels, plus folio-oriented conveniences that resolve the enclosing zone or node from the compound page and scale the adjustment by its page count or by an explicit count, in both protected and unprotected flavors.

Least-recently-used vector accounting is expressed entirely as node occupancy changes. Callers supply either a page, a compound page, or a vector descriptor together with a statistic selector and a signed amount; the implementation resolves the owning node and applies the delta there. Add and subtract conveniences derive the magnitude from the compound page size.

Human-readable labels for zone occupancy, locality events, node statistics and virtual-memory events come from one shared ordered text repository. Each family uses a distinct base offset derived from the sizes of preceding families, with the event family additionally skipping an intermediate block. Least-recently-used list labels reuse the node label lookup at a fixed base plus list index and then omit a short leading prefix.

Writeback coordination uses a descriptor that separates caller-visible requests from engine-internal cursor state. The visible portion carries a remaining work budget, a skipped count, an optional byte interval with cyclic and tagging controls, a synchronization selector, and purpose flags for periodic, background, full-sync and ownership handling. The internal portion carries a small batch buffer, a resume index and a retained error, with an optional cgroup extension that records the issuing writeback context, target file object and foreign-entity detection progress.

Synchronization selection for writeback is a two-valued ordered enumeration. The lower value requests no waiting and the upper value requests waiting across mappings; the two selectors are WB_SYNC_NONE and WB_SYNC_ALL in that order.

Derivation helpers translate a writeback request into lower-layer decisions. A flag mapper yields synchronous versus background block hints from the synchronization selector and purpose flags. A tag mapper chooses between a pinned to-write tag and a dirty tag based on full synchronization or tagging control. A cgroup mapper resolves the block group context from the issuing writeback context when present and otherwise falls back to the root context, with a bio initializer that applies that resolution only when a writeback context is attached.

Writeback domain state combines mutual exclusion with proportional sharing and limit tracking. It holds a spin-based guard, a global floating proportion of completion events, a periodic timer with its interval for aging those proportions, and a timestamped ceiling used to glide toward a reduced dirty threshold after sudden shrinkage of reclaimable memory.

The domain guard serializes updates to the timestamped ceiling fields. A size-change notifier acquires the guard, stamps the current tick count and clears the ceiling, then releases the guard; all other readers and writers of those two fields must hold the same guard.

Throttling state captures both system-wide and per-writeback pressure. It optionally links a domain and its global counterpart in cgroup builds, always points at the target writeback context and its processor-local completion share, records reclaimable capacity alongside current dirtiness and three system thresholds for throttling start, background start and hard ceiling, mirrors the latter three for the specific writeback context, and adds a computed position ratio plus flags for unrestricted running and for exceeded dirtiness.

File-to-writeback association has enabled and disabled shapes. When enabled, attachment binds a file object to a writeback context on first use via a helper owned elsewhere, and detachment warns if the clearing marker is absent before dropping the reference and clearing the pointer. When disabled, attachment, detachment, inode association for synchronous writes, inode detachment, bio initialization, ownership accounting and unmount cleanup are all inert.

Compressed-memory pool statistics expose a single monotonically increasing count of pages reclaimed through compaction. Swap-cache vector state, when enabled, is a descriptor holding a single atomic tally of disk-originated swap-ins used to penalize prior over-reclaim; when disabled the descriptor is empty and all store, load, invalidation, online, offline, initialization, swap-in notification and enablement queries collapse to fixed false, missing-entry, success or no-op answers.

Allocation tagging uses a fixed pseudo-file label, a virtual mapping reservation sized for one hundred thousand tag descriptors, and helpers that bracket a named section by start and stop markers. Profiling support defaults differ by build, with one shape initially enabled and another initially disabled, and a query reports permanent disablement as the negation of that support flag. A shared per-processor counter block provides fallback accounting.

Dirty-throttle scope width is eight. The asynchronous backing-device indicator occupies the lowest bit. Minimum writeback batch is defined from a four-kilobyte base shifted by the difference between the page shift and ten, so larger pages yield smaller page counts.

Negative intermediate tallies can arise from concurrent updates and are masked to zero by most readers, so callers must not interpret a zero as proof of emptiness and must use the monotonic reader when wraparound-free progress matters. Snapshot aggregation walks online processors without holding zone exclusion, so it may observe a moving total. Detaching a file object that lacks the clearing marker triggers a one-time warning path.

In this configuration several operations are intentionally degenerate. Public increment, decrement and modify entry points alias directly to their unprotected variants. Threshold installation, threshold refresh, per-processor folding, quiescing, workqueue flushing and per-zone draining are empty. Combined zone-node summation for a node delegates to the global zone aggregate, and node page queries delegate to a global node helper, while folding of locality events is empty.
Three headers provide idempotent inclusion guards that define a unique marker on first inclusion to suppress repeated processing.
